excerpt: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents TL;DR QDA brings a coding agent into LLM quantization design. For each model and precision, the agent designs the post-training quantization recipe on its own, with no human in the loop. Its checkpoints beat the strongest public recipe on four reasoning models, by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, and run on existing kernels with no inference overhead. The agent works the way a quantization expert does: it proposes a recipe, builds it, measures it and decides what to change next. Two things make this loop fast enough for up to 36 candidates in one eight-hour search: a KL score that takes minutes instead of dozens of GPU-hours, and a library of 21 PTQ methods that stack in any order. We find that no method wins everywhere: the best recipe differs for every model and precision, and the agent finds it by searching. On the 320B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4, one 6.5-hour, $69 search recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for NVIDIA's release. The tools matter too: given NVIDIA ModelOpt's tools instead of ours, the same agent falls 0.5–1.3 points behind on Qwen3.6-35B. A search costs $19–75 of agent tokens. 1An old question In 2024, Yujun Lin, Xingyang's wonderful mentor at MIT HAN Lab, wrote DeepCompressor, the quantization toolbox behind QServe and SVDQuant. He once told us that the results sometimes puzzled him: a new method that looks strong in its paper often adds little once it is stacked on a few basics, such as AWQ's smoothing, a Hadamard rotation and GPTQ. Moreover, nobody knew which methods work well together, because each is tested on its own. Answering that by hand means trying combinations model by model, which no one has time for. Today, however, LLMs can act as optimizers[1, 2], and agent harnesses such as Humanize[3] keep a coding agent working for hours with no one watching.
